query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a controlled boron addition (~0.1 at.%) to the as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy will improve the grain-boundary cohesion and refine the lamellar structure, thereby simultaneously increasing yield strength and enhancing room-temperature tensile ductility relative to the undoped baseline lamellar-colony microstructure.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with two-phase lamellar colonies prone to microcracking at lamellar or interphase boundaries.
generation.intervention: Add a small concentration (≈0.1 at.%) of boron to the alloy composition, ensuring it segregates to colony boundaries.
generation.conditions: Standard vacuum induction melting and homogenization of the alloy, followed by conventional casting into lamellar microstructures. Boron content is controlled to avoid second-phase embrittlement.
generation.structural_mediator: Boron segregation at interfacial boundaries between the lamellar phases
generation.mechanism: Boron enhances boundary cohesion by reducing interfacial energy and impedes microcrack initiation, while mild solid-solution strengthening provides a concurrent increase in yield strength. The reduction in nucleation sites for cracks facilitates improved tensile elongation at room temperature.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the undoped eutectic high-entropy alloy, the boron-doped version will exhibit moderate but measurable increases in yield strength (e.g., ~10% higher) while also providing a significant increase in tensile elongation (e.g., ~50% higher), indicating improved room-temperature ductility alongside boosted strength.
generation.baseline: The unmodified as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies lacking boron addition, displaying limited tensile ductility and susceptibility to microcracking at lamellar boundaries.
generation.boundary: Exceeding a critical boron threshold (e.g., >0.3 at.%) may lead to detrimental boride formation or increased brittleness, negating the positive effects of boundary cohesion. Temperature cycling above typical annealing ranges may also disrupt boron’s beneficial segregation.
generation.uncertainty: While small boron additions can improve boundary integrity in many alloys, the exact optimal range to avoid brittle precipitates needs further validation. Effects on phase stability also warrant additional study.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of eutectic high-entropy alloys using an identical composition except for the controlled boron addition in one set. Perform room-temperature uniaxial tensile tests on dog-bone specimens from both sets alongside microstructural characterization by SEM/TEM to confirm boron segregation and assess microcrack nucleation sites.
measurements: Room-temperature yield strength, ultimate tensile strength, and elongation to failure
Microscopy of fracture surfaces to identify changes in microcrack initiation sites and boundary cohesion
Compositional analysis (e.g., EDS) to verify boron distribution at interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If samples with boron addition exhibit either no stronger boundary cohesion, no improvement in ductility, or no increase in yield strength compared to baseline samples, or if unexpected brittle phases form that negate gains in ductility, the hypothesis is falsified.
